newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan says it is winning, Egypt refuses help.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says it is winning, Egypt refuses help.

text.p: The Sudanese army said on Saturday it was winning the war in the east of the country and preparing to drive out what it says are foreign invaders.
But neighbouring Egypt said it had refused to help the Sudanese government fight off the attacks because they were an internal matter, nothing to do with Ethiopia or Eritrea.

Armed forces spokesman Mohamad al-Sanoussi Ahmad told a news briefing in Khartoum that fighting continued but the fronts were now stable. "The situation is under control to a large degree... When we say stable, it does not mean there is no fighting. It means that nothing significant has taken place," he added.
"The army is dominating in the battlefield and it is preparing to repel the attack on Sudan," he said.
In public Sudanese officials say Ethiopian and Eritrean forces have done most of the fighting but the opposition in exile says its rebel forces are wholly responsible.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, in his first comment on Sudanese events since the army came under attack in the Blue Nile and Kassala areas last Sunday, said Sudan had asked him for financial and military help against the offensive.
Mubarak, at a meeting with intellectuals in Cairo, was answering a question about his talks on Thursday with Sudanese Vice-President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh.
"How can I support them when they are squabbling with the Sudanese people and there are Sudanese in opposition?" Mubarak said. "How can Egypt intervene and hit the Sudanese?"
"The truth is there is no Eritrean or Ethiopian attack or any foreign attack. We have asked and we're sure of that. No one has entered Sudanese territory," he added.

Even Saleh, who spent two days in Cairo this week, had told him that Ethiopian and Eritrean forces were operating from outside Sudan, he said. "I gave him (Saleh) some tough talk, politely," Mubarak added.

Neither side gave fresh and detailed information on Saturday about the latest fighting but a government newspaper said the army had pushed back the attacks on the southern Blue Nile front, where the rebels have the towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan.
"The armed forces have made a big advance at the battle fronts," said the government newspaper al-Sudan al-Hadith.
"They have confined the Tigrean (Ethiopian) forces to a narrow area to the west of the towns of Kurmuk and Qeissan, forcing the Tigrean forces to retreat to rear positions."
In Cairo the opposition National Democratic Alliance (NDA), denied the government's claim of advances. "They are liars," said opposition spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa.

The government newspaper said the Sudanese air force had bombarded areas lost by the army and that the Ethiopians were preparing to hand over their positions to south Sudanese rebels flown into Ethiopia from Uganda and Eritrea.
The NDA said Antonov bombers of the Sudanese air force on Friday bombed a rebel-held area near the border settlement of Menze, which is also in Blue Nile state.
"We appeal to the international community and humanitarian organisations to provide humanitarian assistance to the people of the area," said statement by the NDA's military forces.
In Geneva, Swiss-based Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said on Friday Antonov bombers, helicopter gunships and ground troops had been razing villages in Blue Nile state.
But the armed forces spokesman denied the Sudanese planes had done any bombing in the area.
"If they are Sudanese planes, they are there for reconnaissance, to determine the positions and movement of the other side," General Ahmad said.

The government spokesman, Brigadier al-Tayeb Ibrahim Khair, confirmed that the commissioner of Kurmuk, Yaaqoub Hussein, and other local officials had been taken prisoner. He appealed to the international community to ensure his safety and have him returned to his home.
Unlike Egypt two other Arab countries, Iraq and Jordan, have adopted the Sudanese view of events.
Jordan on Friday urged Arab states to come to Sudan's aid, saying it faced a plot against its territorial unity.
Jordan's Moslem Brotherhood said in a statement on Saturday that the Sudanese rebels were part of a U.S.-Israeli conspiracy to thwart Moslems and plant a Zionist state in Africa.
